mcqs.question: Why did idioms like map/filter and Optional spread to mainstream languages while pure FP languages like Haskell stayed comparatively niche?
options: An idiom can be adopted one call site at a time, incrementally, while switching a whole codebase and team to a new language is a far larger, rarely-accepted cost
Haskell and similar languages are strictly slower at runtime than mainstream languages
Mainstream languages copied the idioms because Haskell's syntax was considered too readable to differentiate from
Pure FP languages never implemented map or filter, so mainstream languages had to invent their own versions independently
mcqs.explanation: The adoption cost is the real differentiator: a team can start using an idiom like Optional in new code today without touching anything else, whereas a full language switch requires rehiring, retraining, and rewriting. Runtime speed isn't the deciding factor, readability comparisons aren't the driver, and Haskell has long had these exact constructs — mainstream languages borrowed the ideas rather than reinventing them from scratch.

mcqs.question: Java added lambdas and Streams in Java 8. Which FP idea did Java deliberately NOT adopt alongside them?
options: First-class function values
The map/filter/reduce vocabulary for collection pipelines
Purity enforcement — a Java lambda can still mutate captured state, and collections remain mutable by default
Fluent method chaining syntax
mcqs.explanation: Java 8 added first-class functions, the map/filter/reduce vocabulary via Streams, and fluent chaining, but deliberately left mutability and purity unenforced — a lambda can still close over and mutate external state, and collections stay mutable unless explicitly wrapped. It borrowed the useful mechanics without requiring the paradigm shift.

mcqs.question: Which of these is true about Python's relationship to tail-call optimization?
options: Python enforces tail-call optimization for all recursive functions automatically
Python implements TCO only inside generator functions, not regular ones
CPython deliberately does not implement TCO at all, so deep tail-recursive Python code still risks a RecursionError regardless of how it's structured
Python delegates TCO to the operating system's stack management
mcqs.explanation: CPython's maintainers have been explicit that TCO is intentionally not implemented, in part because it would make tracebacks harder to follow — so writing a function in tail-recursive form doesn't protect it from stack overflow in Python, consistent with what the recursion topic in this group covers. There's no generator-specific exception and no OS-level delegation involved.

mcqs.question: What distinguishes Kotlin and Scala's approach to FP from Java's?
options: They were designed from the start as multi-paradigm languages, with FP idioms as first-class citizens alongside full OOP interop, rather than idioms bolted onto an existing OOP-only language later
They removed object-oriented features entirely in favor of pure functional style
They run on a different, FP-specific virtual machine incompatible with Java bytecode
They only support FP idioms in a separate file type distinct from their OOP code
mcqs.explanation: Kotlin and Scala baked FP idioms — sealed classes with exhaustive matching, immutable-by-default case classes, first-class functor/monad support — into the language design alongside full OOP, letting a codebase mix both styles freely. Neither language removed OOP, both run on the JVM (Scala explicitly interoperates with Java), and there's no separate file type required for either paradigm.

mcqs.question: A team mandates "no more for-loops, everything must be a functional pipeline" all at once. What's the predicted failure mode described in this slide?
options: The codebase will fail to compile until every loop is converted

Code review slows down and incident response gets harder, because teammates unfamiliar with the idioms have to learn the pattern while also checking correctness, and stack traces through deep composition hide which stage failed
The runtime will silently reject any remaining imperative code
Nothing changes in practice — the mandate has no real effect on team velocity
mcqs.explanation: The described failure is about human and process cost — reviewers doing double duty (learning plus verifying), and production debugging losing visibility into which composed stage failed — not a technical compile-time or runtime rejection, and it's explicitly not a non-event; velocity is the thing that suffers.

mcqs.question: In the refactored Streams pipeline, the original condition isActive() && getEmail() != null was split into two separate filter() calls instead of kept as one combined predicate. What's the benefit of that split?
options: It makes the stream execute in parallel automatically
It removes the need for the final collect() call
It changes the result to include inactive users as well
Each stage reads as one clear, independent check, and the null guard sits right next to the operation it protects instead of being bundled into a distant compound condition
mcqs.explanation: Splitting into separate stages is a readability and locality improvement — each filter states one condition, and the null check is positioned right before the operation that would fail on null. It has no effect on parallelism, doesn't remove the need to collect results, and doesn't change which users are included versus the original combined condition.
